body.text: Pakistan is renowned for delivering one political surprise after another. Marred by several military coups, its political history is unique in that not a single Prime Minister has ever completed a full five-year term.

Paradoxically, the only consistent feature of Pakistan’s domestic and foreign policies is its persistent impulsiveness. The friction between the Union and State governments is systemic, with clashing policies and public finger-pointing over national security exposing deep structural deficits in governance.

The federal leadership, along with the country’s powerful military establishment, boasts on the one hand about its self-proclaimed, growing role in global affairs, most famously its role in negotiating between the US and Iran. They never get tired of the often-repeated claim that the country is fighting a long war on terrorism and has paid an irreparable price for it.

On the other hand, the country has been unable to resolve its conflict with Afghanistan and its former ally, the Afghan Taliban. As a matter of fact, Islamabad carried out military strikes and launched a full-fledged military operation in February-March to coerce the Afghan Taliban into submission, a mission in which it miserably failed.

It is also unable to curb armed attacks in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. An upsurge in armed attacks by the Baloch rebels and the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) is challenging the country’s security establishment and making it pay a heavy price.
A prolonged political crisis

There is also the long-festering political crisis, with no sign that the confrontation between the ruling regime and the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) will be resolved any time soon. All efforts of the ruling coalition comprising the Pakistan Muslim League (PML-N), the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP), and the military have failed to dent the popular support enjoyed by Imran Khan and his party. This not only emboldens Imran and his party but also creates incentives for continuing the confrontational approach.

Two new major controversies have now erupted. One concerns a piece of news—later confirmed by the government and the military as well—that a plan is under consideration to form new provinces in the country. Although it is an old issue that resurfaces from time to time in government and public debates, it gained momentum when Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad, said, "The system we have been living under has collapsed."

This was a strong statement, coming from a Minister close to the military establishment. Naqvi is in the Cabinet without contesting elections; he is a military appointee. He was the Caretaker Chief Minister of Punjab from January 22, 2023, to February 26, 2024. After being appointed Interior Minister by the military (therefore called “Rawalpindi’s man” by a PPP leader), Naqvi has been throwing his weight behind the policies of the military establishment.

In August 2024, he claimed that a Station House Officer was enough to eliminate terrorism in the country. Since then, not only have armed attacks increased but have also started taking a heavy toll on the security forces. Balochistan has seen a persistent rise in armed attacks, as the latest data shows. Also, Naqvi continues to be the chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) at a time when the national cricket team has been drawing flak for poor performance.

Still, no one dares to question Naqvi or his capabilities, a clear sign that he enjoys the backing of the military establishment. So, when he said that “all political parties should sit together in a single room, whether for a day, month or year. They will have to settle every issue of their country, including new units and provinces,” his remarks were perceived as reflecting the thinking of the military establishment.

This view was further strengthened by the statement of Director General Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, who said: “As a primary stakeholder in security, we [the military] would like to say that good governance is the key to security and stability. Without that, your issues cannot be solved.”

Seen through the lenses of security and the overall situation in Pakistan, the statement suggested two possible scenarios. One, the current regime is unable to address the country’s growing security and administrative problems. Acknowledging this publicly implies that all attempts to stem them have failed. Second, despite its big claims, the military establishment has no clue about how to contain the armed attacks in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Now, excuses are being concocted to remove the PTI-led government in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa.

The contradiction was further underlined by another controversy. Chief Minister of Punjab Maryam Nawaz recently said that “the threat is less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces. Terrorism comes from there to Punjab. Everyone has an eye on Punjab.” Maryam Nawaz is the daughter of former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and niece of the current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

As Chief Minister of Pakistan’s largest province, she not only acknowledged that the security institutions had failed to contain armed attacks in the country, but also appeared to suggest that her province saw itself as being different from the other three provinces.
Military facing the heat

What message was Maryam trying to send? Was it a response to the proposal that new provinces should be carved out of existing provinces that have failed to ensure security and governance? Or was it a hint of the role of political violence in the country’s domestic politics, which parties use to retain their support?

Expectedly, Maryam’s statement drew serious condemnation across the political spectrum. The PTI, which rules the violence-ridden Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, said that the problem for Maryam lay not in the neighbouring provinces but in her “own mindset and priorities”.

Nawaz Sharif was the blue-eyed boy of the military dictator Zia-ul-Haq. He was serving as the Chief Minister of Punjab when terrorism reportedly took root in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa; Sharif ruled Punjab with military support. Zia had sponsored armed groups for use in Afghanistan. Today, those same armed groups have turned their guns towards Pakistan.According to the renowned journalist Saleem Safi, the majority of the terrorist groups and their leadership came from Punjab and were not Pashtuns or Balochis, underlining the point that the PML-N policy might have facilitated terrorism in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa.

If terrorism indeed originates from the neighbouring provinces of Punjab, what is the Punjabi-dominated federal government and, more importantly, the country’s Punjabi-dominated powerful military, doing? Aren’t the statements of various leaders a tacit acknowledgement that Pakistan’s military has failed to resolve the problem of armed violence in the country?

In any case, the military establishment in Pakistan seems to be facing the heat. The factors behind these developments somehow point back to the military establishment. Still, the government does not appear to be seeking answers or trying for any course correction.
The reality is that the ruling elite of Pakistan has no consistency in its domestic or foreign policy. And, in all likelihood, these issues will continue to haunt the country.
Nazir Ahmad Mir has a PhD in conflict analysis and peace building and is a research fellow at the Centre for Peace Studies in New Delhi.
